stem: A 60-year-old man who smokes heavily has cough, weakness, leg swelling and a potassium of 2.8 mEq/L. Morning cortisol and ACTH are both high, and ACTH does not fall with high-dose dexamethasone. Chest CT shows a central mass at the hilum, and a bronchoscopic biopsy is taken.
oneliner: 60M + heavy smoker + hilar mass + hypokalemia + edema + high ACTH not suppressed by dexamethasone → which histologic appearance?

options.A: Polygonal cells with keratin pearls and intercellular bridges
options.C: Small dark cells with scant cytoplasm, molded nuclei and crush artifact
options.D: Pleural-based sheets of epithelioid and spindle cells
options.E: Huge pleomorphic cells with no differentiation

whyNot.A: **Keratin pearls** mean squamous cell carcinoma, central too, but typically causing PTHrP hypercalcemia, not ectopic ACTH
whyNot.D: **Mesothelioma** encases the lung along the pleura after asbestos; it does not form a hilar mass that secretes ACTH
whyNot.E: **Large cell carcinoma** has bizarre pleomorphic cells and is usually peripheral

answer: Small blue cells with nuclear molding and crush artifact
why: A central tumor with **ectopic ACTH** (hypokalemia, no suppression by dexamethasone) in a smoker is **small cell lung carcinoma**, a **neuroendocrine** tumor. Fragile **small cells with scant cytoplasm, molding and crush artifact** are the hallmark; it is chromogranin and synaptophysin positive.

idea.rule: Central smoker's tumor with ectopic hormones shows small crushed cells with molded nuclei.
also: SIADH (hyponatremia) and Lambert-Eaton syndrome
Amplification of MYC
Rapid growth, early metastasis and initial chemotherapy response

stem: A 20-year-old woman with no past illness dies instantly in a car crash, and her lung tissue is examined under the microscope. The alveolar septa are thin, with capillaries pressed against a continuous lining.
oneliner: 20F + healthy lung from a car-crash death + thin alveolar septa lined by a continuous layer → which cell covers most of the alveolar surface?
ask: Which cell type covers most of the alveolar surface?

whyNot.B: Type II cells are cuboidal, make **surfactant** and cover only a **small fraction** of the surface
whyNot.C: Macrophages are **free cells** in the air spaces, not part of the **lining**
whyNot.D: Club cells are **bronchiolar** secretory cells, not alveolar lining cells
whyNot.E: Fibroblasts sit in the **interstitium** of the septum, beneath the lining

why: **Type I pneumocytes** are very thin squamous cells that cover about **95%** of the alveolar surface and form the **blood-air barrier** with the capillary endothelium. **Type II** cells are cuboidal, make **surfactant** and can regenerate type I cells.

idea.rule: Type I pneumocytes cover about 95% of the surface for gas exchange; type II cells cover the rest, make surfactant and repair the lining.
also: Type II cells proliferate and replace damaged type I cells
Type I cells are fragile, so they are lost in diffuse alveolar damage
The blood-air barrier is type I cell, fused basement membrane and capillary endothelium
Type II cells contain lamellar bodies that store surfactant

stem: A 66-year-old man has had two years of dry cough and breathlessness. He has digital clubbing and fine end-inspiratory crackles at both bases. Spirometry shows a restrictive pattern with a low diffusing capacity, and CT shows honeycombing at the periphery of the lower lungs.
oneliner: 66M + 2 years dry cough and dyspnea + clubbing + basal crackles + restrictive with low DLCO + peripheral basal honeycombing → which biopsy finding?
ask: Which lung biopsy finding is expected?

options.B: Uniform hyaline membranes lining the alveolar walls
options.C: Poorly formed granulomas clustered around bronchioles
options.D: Destroyed alveolar walls with no scarring
options.E: Patchy subpleural scarring with fibroblastic foci

whyNot.A: Granulomas along lymphatics suggest **sarcoidosis** with hilar nodes, not **peripheral honeycombing**
whyNot.B: Hyaline membranes mean **acute diffuse alveolar damage** with abrupt onset, not a **two-year** course
whyNot.C: Loose peribronchiolar granulomas suggest **hypersensitivity pneumonitis** after an inhaled antigen, none given here
whyNot.D: Alveolar wall destruction without scarring is **emphysema**, an **obstructive** pattern, not a **restrictive** one

answer: Usual interstitial pneumonia: patchy subpleural fibrosis, fibroblastic foci, honeycombing
why: Progressive dyspnea, **clubbing**, **basal crackles**, a **restrictive** pattern with **low DLCO** and **basal honeycombing** point to **idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis**. Its histology is **usual interstitial pneumonia**: patchy subpleural scar of different ages beside normal lung, with **fibroblastic foci** and honeycomb change.

idea.rule: IPF = usual interstitial pneumonia: patchy, subpleural, basal fibrosis of mixed age.
also: Restrictive disease gives low FVC, a normal or high FEV1/FVC ratio and low DLCO
Repeated alveolar epithelial injury drives TGF-beta-mediated fibroblast activation
Velcro crackles and clubbing are typical
Honeycombing is the end stage of fibrosis

stem: A 50-year-old man who keeps parakeets in his bedroom has cough and breathlessness that return in the evenings at home and ease when he is away on trips. CT shows patchy ground-glass opacities in the mid and upper zones with air trapping, and lavage fluid is rich in lymphocytes.
oneliner: 50M + parakeets at home + cough and dyspnea that ease when away + mid-upper ground-glass with air trapping + lymphocytic lavage → which biopsy finding?
ask: Which lung biopsy finding is expected?

options.B: Loose, poorly formed granulomas around bronchioles
options.C: Caseating granulomas with Langhans giant cells

whyNot.A: Tight granulomas along lymphatics suggest **sarcoidosis**, which has no link to **exposure that comes and goes**
whyNot.C: Caseating granulomas mean **tuberculosis**, with fever, weight loss and cavities, not an **exposure-linked** illness
whyNot.D: Fibroblastic foci with honeycombing are **usual interstitial pneumonia**, a basal disease with no **exposure pattern**
whyNot.E: Hyaline membranes mean **acute diffuse alveolar damage**, not months of exposure-related symptoms

answer: Bronchiolocentric lymphocytic inflammation with poorly formed noncaseating granulomas
why: Symptoms that **ease away from home**, a **bird** at home, **upper-zone ground-glass** with **air trapping** and **lymphocytic lavage** indicate **hypersensitivity pneumonitis** (a mixed type III and IV reaction). Histology shows **lymphocytes around bronchioles** with **loose, poorly formed granulomas**.

idea.rule: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis = bronchiolocentric lymphocytes plus loose granulomas; remove the antigen.
also: Bird fancier's lung and farmer's lung are classic examples
It is a mixed type III and type IV hypersensitivity reaction
Acute attacks follow exposure by hours; chronic exposure leads to fibrosis
It is not IgE-mediated, unlike asthma

stem: A 6-year-old girl has had hoarseness since toddlerhood and now has noisy breathing when she breathes in. Laryngoscopy shows several pink, warty growths on both vocal cords. Similar growths were removed twice before and came back, and her mother had genital warts when she was born.
oneliner: 6F + hoarseness since toddlerhood + inspiratory stridor + warty vocal cord growths that recur + mother with genital warts → which histologic appearance?
ask: Which histologic appearance is expected on biopsy?

options.A: Keratin pearls invading below the basement membrane
options.B: Small blue cells with nuclear molding
options.C: Branching papillae with benign squamous covering
options.D: Fibrinoid necrosis of small vessel walls

whyNot.A: Invasive keratinizing cells mean **squamous carcinoma**, which is rare at this age and not **multiple, recurrent warts**
whyNot.B: Small blue cells with molding mean **small cell carcinoma**, a tumor of heavy smokers
whyNot.D: Fibrinoid necrosis of vessels is **vasculitis**, with nasal and kidney involvement, not **warty growths**
whyNot.E: Nests of uniform neuroendocrine cells mean a **carcinoid**, a solitary tumor, not **multiple warty lesions**

answer: Squamous papilloma: papillae with fibrovascular cores, benign epithelium (HPV 6 and 11)
why: **Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis** follows **HPV 6 and 11** passed from a mother with **genital warts** at birth. The growths are benign **squamous papillomas**: branching papillae with **fibrovascular cores** under non-malignant squamous epithelium. They **recur** after removal.

idea.rule: HPV 6 and 11 cause benign papillomas and warts; HPV 16 and 18 cause carcinoma.
also: Transmission is vertical during vaginal delivery
Koilocytes may be seen in the squamous cells
Hoarseness and stridor in a child suggest laryngeal papillomas
Rarely a papilloma turns into squamous carcinoma

stem: A 52-year-old woman who has never smoked has a 2-cm smooth nodule found on a routine chest x-ray. She has no symptoms. The excised nodule shows nests of uniform round cells with rare mitoses and no necrosis, and the cells stain for chromogranin.
oneliner: 52F + never-smoker + asymptomatic 2-cm lung nodule + uniform nests with rare mitoses, no necrosis + chromogranin positive → which electron microscopy finding?
ask: Which finding on electron microscopy is expected in the tumor cells?

whyNot.A: Long slender microvilli mark **mesothelioma**, a tumor of the pleura, not a **well-circumscribed lung nodule**
whyNot.B: Tonofilaments with desmosomes mean **squamous differentiation**, with keratin and necrosis, not **chromogranin-positive** nests
whyNot.C: Birbeck granules mark **Langerhans cell histiocytosis** (CD1a and S100 positive), not a **chromogranin-positive** tumor
whyNot.E: Mucin droplets mean **adenocarcinoma**, with glands, not **uniform neuroendocrine nests**

why: Uniform nests with **rare mitoses**, **no necrosis** and **chromogranin** positivity make a **bronchial carcinoid**, a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor. Its cells contain **dense-core, membrane-bound neurosecretory granules** on electron microscopy.

idea.rule: Neuroendocrine tumors (carcinoid, small cell) carry dense-core neurosecretory granules and stain for chromogranin.
also: Neuroendocrine cells are Kulchitsky cells of the bronchial epithelium
Carcinoid is not related to smoking
Small cell carcinoma has the same granules but marked necrosis and mitoses
Carcinoid syndrome appears mainly with liver metastases

stem: A 70-year-old retired shipyard worker has a thick, firm white rind encasing the right lung. He has a bloody pleural effusion and calcified pleural plaques, and the tumor cells stain for calretinin.
oneliner: 70M + former shipyard worker + white pleural rind around right lung + bloody effusion + calcified plaques + calretinin positive → which electron microscopy finding?
ask: Which finding on electron microscopy is expected in the tumor cells?

options.A: Short, stubby microvilli with mucin vacuoles

whyNot.A: Short stubby microvilli with mucin point to **adenocarcinoma**, which is **calretinin negative** and does not encase the pleura
whyNot.B: Dense-core granules mark **neuroendocrine tumors**, which are **chromogranin positive**, not **calretinin positive**
whyNot.C: Tonofilaments with desmosomes mean **squamous cell carcinoma**, an airway tumor, not a **pleural rind**
whyNot.D: Lamellar bodies are the surfactant stores of **type II pneumocytes**, not a feature of a **pleural** tumor

why: A **pleural rind** with **asbestos exposure**, **plaques**, a **bloody effusion** and **calretinin** positivity is **malignant mesothelioma**. On electron microscopy the cells have **long, slender, bushy microvilli**, unlike the **short stubby** microvilli of adenocarcinoma.

idea.rule: Mesothelioma has long, slender microvilli and is calretinin positive; adenocarcinoma has short microvilli and mucin.
also: Asbestos exposure appears decades before the tumor
Mesothelioma cells stain for calretinin, WT-1 and cytokeratin 5/6
Bloody pleural effusion and chest pain are typical
Pleural plaques mark asbestos exposure but are not themselves precancerous

stem: A 19-year-old woman with eczema has episodic wheeze triggered by cats and cold air. Her FEV1 rises after inhaled albuterol, and her blood eosinophil count is raised. During an attack she coughs up thick mucus plugs, which are sent for microscopy.
oneliner: 19F + eczema + wheeze with cats and cold air + FEV1 rises after albuterol + eosinophilia + thick mucus plugs → which sputum finding?
ask: What does microscopy of the sputum most likely show?

options.A: Spiral mucus casts with needle-shaped crystals
options.B: Golden-brown beaded rods with a clear center
options.C: Macrophages filled with brown iron pigment
options.E: Acid-fast rods with a beaded outline

whyNot.B: Beaded **asbestos bodies** need an occupational **asbestos exposure**, which she lacks
whyNot.C: Iron-laden macrophages mean **alveolar hemorrhage or heart failure**, not an **atopic** illness
whyNot.D: Lancet-shaped diplococci mean **pneumococcal pneumonia** with fever and productive cough, not **episodic** wheeze
whyNot.E: Acid-fast rods mean **tuberculosis**, with weight loss and chronic cough, not **reversible** wheeze

why: **Episodic, reversible** wheeze with **atopy** and **eosinophilia** is **asthma**. Sputum shows **Curschmann spirals** (whorled mucus casts of shed epithelium) and **Charcot-Leyden crystals**, formed from **eosinophil** protein.

idea.rule: Asthma sputum = Curschmann spirals + Charcot-Leyden crystals + eosinophils.
also: Charcot-Leyden crystals come from eosinophil galectin-10
Eosinophil major basic protein damages bronchial epithelium
Mucus plugging and smooth muscle hypertrophy narrow the airway
Atopic asthma is a type I hypersensitivity reaction
